newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan capital enjoys first night of calm in days.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan capital enjoys first night of calm in days.

text.p: The Kenyan capital enjoyed its first calm night since Sunday after the government of President Daniel arap Moi closed down Nairobi University following violent clashes between students and police.
Business and financial leaders were cautiously optimistic that normality would return to the city after unrest this week linked to a campaign for constitutional reform.
Nine people were killed in Kenya on Monday during the most violent clashes between police and protesters since a violent campaign in July 1990 that helped persuade Moi to allow multi-party politics.
Political analysts expected the capital to quieten down after the closure of Nairobi University, which has 19,000 students and is known to back most opposition demands.

The closure of Nairobi University was triggered by students streaming into Nairobi streets to mourn four colleagues the independent Daily Nation newspaper reported had died in the protests on Monday. Police denied the Daily Nation report.

Nairobi University students have been caught up in a wave of varied protests since last week when they stoned motorists and looted shops during a march against a new education bill that provides for expulsion of students who cannot pay their fees.
On Monday they joined the demonstrations called by a coalition seeking constitutional reforms before parliamentary and presidential elections due later this year.
"Without the students, I believe the city will be quieter and a major armour has been taken out of the reform movement, at least for the moment," a business leader said.
Kenyatta University, near the capital, is in recess.

The Daily Nation report also sparked disturbances on Wednesday at Egerton University, Kenya's premier agricultural school based in the Rift Valley, but calm returned there as night fell and the institution was expected to remain open.

Opposition parties, human rights and church groups in the National Convention Executive Committee (NCEC) had said they would demonstrate on Wednesday at a regional summit in Nairobi -- held to discuss the conflict in Sudan -- to bring Kenya to the attention of visiting leaders.

But they did not carry out their threat. Opposition leaders were thrown out of a Nairobi hotel by police late on Wednesday where one president was staying when they tried to send their petition to his suite.
NCEC member Charles Maranga said the coalition was taking stock of the week's events before taking further measures.

Thirteen European Union member states, the European Commission, Canada, Cyprus, the Czech Republic, Japan, Norway and Switzerland condemned the violence and urged the government to start talks with pro-reform groups.
"It is the responsibility of the government of Kenya to protect not only the safety of Kenyan citizens but also their human and civil rights," the embassies said in a statement.

Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) Governor Micah Cheserem said the shilling had taken some beating on market jitters after unrest from Monday but that the phenomenon was temporary. He said he saw sanity prevailing on both sides of the political divide.
The shilling slipped to around 56.50/65 versus the dollar on Wednesday compared to 54.90 at close on Friday last week.

Reformists want the repeal of six laws from colonial times including the Public Order Act used to regulate public gatherings. They also demand free access to state-controlled media, particularly radio, and changes in the electoral law.
No date has been set for the parliamentary and presidential polls in which Moi, 73, is still widely expected to win another five-year term because of squabbling among opposition leaders.

On Tuesday, Kenyan opposition legislator Charity Kaluki Ngilu launched her presidential campaign by offering herself as a one-term "bridge" to ensure constitutional reforms that clear the way to proper democracy.
In Germany, dissident Moslem preacher and Moi critic, Sheikh Khalid Balala, announced he would return to Kenya on Saturday after two years of forced exile there.
